papers.title_in_file: Advantage of Quantum Machine Learning from General Computational Advantages
papers.version_note: arXiv:2312.03057v1, 5 Dec 2023; main text, Methods, Appendices A to C and references.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that constructs a family of supervised learning tasks over classical data and proves a quantum-versus-classical learning separation for any function in HeurFBQP minus HeurFBPP/poly, with data-preparation protocols.

existing.note: The paper proposes the two-party setup, the data-preparation algorithms and the small-size classical extrapolation; it reports no experiment.
quotes: we also propose to perform B’s task by only using classical computation for several small problem sizes N

existing.note: The formal condition is two-sided and stronger than the stored value says: the function must stay hard for classical algorithms even with a polynomial-length advice string.
existing.value: The authors state that the result applies to a general class of functions that quantum algorithms compute efficiently in polynomial time for a large fraction of inputs and that no classical algorithm computes, and they require the function to remain hard for any classical algorithm even with an arbitrary polynomial-length advice string.
existing.anchor: Introduction p.2; Advantage of QML from general quantum computational advantages, p.3
quotes: for a general class of functions that can be computed efficiently in polynomial time for a large fraction of inputs by quantum algorithms but not by any classical algorithm
remain hard to compute by any classical algorithm even with an arbitrary polynomial-length advice string
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its result (Introduction p.2 and the definition of the function class, p.3).

existing.note: The stored value is a fragment of Theorem 1. The theorem also states quantum efficient learnability and a quantumly efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class, under any target distribution; the proofs are Theorems 12, 13 and 14 in Appendix B.
existing.value: The paper states, as its main theorem, that under any target distribution over N-bit inputs, for any quantumly advantageous function under that distribution, the concept class is quantumly efficiently learnable, and a quantumly efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class can be constructed for it, while the concept class is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class.
existing.anchor: Theorem 1, main text p.3; proved as Theorems 12, 13, 14 in Appendix B, p.16-19
quotes: Under any target distribution DN over N -bit inputs, for any quantumly advantageous function fN under DN , the concept class CN defined in (2) with fN is quantumly efficiently learnable
By contrast, CN is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class.
existing.certainty_reason: The theorem is stated with its conditions in the main text and proved in Appendix B (Theorems 12, 13, 14).
existing.reader_inference: The classical hardness is conditional on the chosen function being quantumly advantageous; the paper proves no such function exists unconditionally (see the open-problem assertion).

assertions.value: The paper defines a quantumly advantageous function under a distribution as a function that is efficiently computable by a quantum algorithm for a large fraction of inputs drawn from that distribution and is outside the heuristic classical class with advice.
assertions.anchor: Definition 9, Appendix B 1, p.13; main text p.3
quotes: we call fN a quantumly advantageous function under the target distribution DN
we require that fN (x) should be efficiently computable by a quantum algorithm for a large fraction of x drawn from DN

assertions.value: The paper defines the concept class as the set of concepts parameterized by a vector s in the vector space over the two-element field, where each concept labels an input by the bitwise inner product of the input's feature vector with s.
assertions.anchor: Definition 10, Appendix B 1, p.13; main text p.2-3
quotes: we construct our concept class CN = {cs}s parameterized by s in the vector space F2D over a finite field
where fN (x) · s is the bitwise inner product in FD2
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its concept class (Definition 10; equation 2).

assertions.value: The paper proves, as its theorem on quantum learnability, that for any target distribution over the N-bit input space and any quantumly advantageous function, the concept class of Definition 10 is quantumly efficiently learnable by Algorithm 1.
quotes: any target distribution DN over the N -bit input space XN
the concept class CN in Definition 10 with fN is quantumly efficiently learnable by Algorithm 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement and conditions quoted from Theorem 12, with its proof in the same appendix.

assertions.value: The paper states, as its lemma on linear combinations, that for vectors sampled independently from the same distribution on a D-dimensional vector space over the finite field, the (M +1)th vector is a linear combination of the other M vectors with a high probability, which the paper gives as at least one minus D over (M +1).
quotes: Suppose that M vectors y1, . . . , yM ∈ FD2 are sampled from any probability distribution on a D-dimensional vector space FD2 over the finite field
If the (M +1)th vector y is sampled from the same distribution, then y can be represented by a linear combination of the other M vectors
assertions.certainty_reason: Lemma stated with its conditions and proved in Appendix B 2; the bound itself is printed as a display formula that the text layer garbles.

assertions.value: The paper proves, as its theorem on quantum evaluatability, that for any target distribution and any quantumly advantageous function the hypothesis class of the concept class is quantumly efficiently evaluatable by Algorithm 2.
quotes: the hypothesis class HN in (B12) with fN , parameterized by s˜ ∈ FD, is quantumly efficiently evaluatable by Algorithm 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement quoted from Theorem 13; the proof follows it in Appendix B 2.

assertions.value: The paper proves, as its theorem on classical hardness, that for any target distribution and any quantumly advantageous function the concept class is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class.
quotes: the concept class CN in Definition 10 with fN is not classically efficiently learnable by any classically efficiently evaluatable hypothesis class.
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement quoted from Theorem 14; the proof by contradiction follows it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the classical hardness is proved by contradiction using the vector space over the finite field as the feature space: if every concept along the standard basis were classically learnable by classically evaluatable hypotheses, the feature map would be computable by a polynomial-time classical algorithm.
assertions.anchor: Methods, p.8; Algorithm 3 and proof of Theorem 14, Appendix B 3, p.18-20
quotes: our key idea is to use the property of the vector space F2D over the finite field used as the feature space in our construction
would be computed by a polynomialtime classical algorithm using these classical evaluation algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: The proof is given in Appendix B 3 (Algorithm 3 and the proof of Theorem 14).

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum learning algorithm computes the features with a quantum algorithm and then classically performs Gaussian elimination to solve a system of linear equations, and that the solution found may differ from the true parameter yet still gives a correct hypothesis for a large fraction of inputs.
assertions.anchor: Methods, p.7-8; Algorithm 1, Appendix B 2, p.14-15
quotes: Our learning algorithm then classically performs Gaussian elimination to solve a system of linear equations
any of the solutions s˜ of (8) (even if (10) is the case) leads to a correct hypothesis
assertions.certainty_reason: Algorithm 1 and the proof of Theorem 12 in Appendix B 2.

assertions.value: The paper proves, as its theorem on quantum data preparation, that Algorithm 4 outputs the sample data with a high probability within a polynomial time, using the quantum algorithm for the feature map.
quotes: Algorithm 4 outputs the M sample data
with a high probability at least 1 − δ within a polynomial time
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 15 is stated and proved in Appendix C 2.

assertions.value: The paper states that for a concept class built on the inverse of a classically one-way permutation, Algorithm 5 prepares the sample data by a deterministic classical algorithm with no error, in polynomial time.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 18 and its proof, Appendix C 3, p.23-24
quotes: Algorithm 5 is a deterministic algorithm and has no error
the data preparation for our concept class
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 18 and its proof in Appendix C 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the demonstration uses two parties: a party that prepares the classical sample data, and a second party that receives the data and performs the learning.
assertions.anchor: Protocol section, p.5; Appendix C 1, p.21
quotes: a party A is in charge of preparing the classical sample data, and the other party B receives the data from A to perform the learning
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its demonstration setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the target distribution can be any distribution over the N input bits, whereas the earlier Shor-based work allowed only the uniform distribution.
quotes: studied a restricted setting that only allows for a uniform distribution in the choice of the target distribution DN
DN can be an arbitrary distribution over the N bits without this restriction
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its setting (Methods).

assertions.value: The authors state that they study the advantage of QML as a separation between classical learning and evaluation (CC) and quantum learning and evaluation (QQ), constructing a learning task in QQ but not in CC.
quotes: we will study the advantage of QML in the sense of CC / QQ separation
we will construct a learning task in QQ but not in CC
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the sense of separation it proves.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because evaluatability is defined by heuristic complexity, their hardness proof implies the more conventional classical hardness for the worst-case complexity as well.
quotes: our proof of the classical hardness of our learning tasks for the heuristic complexity implies the more conventional classical hardness for the worst-case complexity as well.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Appendix B 3 beside the proof of Theorem 14.

assertions.value: The authors state that, so far, the advantage of QML in supervised learning with classical data has been proven only from the quantum advantage of Shor's algorithms, through cryptographic arguments that depend on the structure of discrete logarithms and integer factoring.
quotes: has been proven only based on the quantum computational advantage of Shor’s algorithms
essentially depending on the specific mathematical structure of discrete logarithms and integer factoring
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about prior work, cited to other papers.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as candidate quantumly advantageous functions, quantum algorithms for topological data analysis, for Pell's equation and for BQP-complete problems; they state these as candidates and do not prove that any of them is quantumly advantageous.
quotes: The functions computed by these quantum algorithms are leading candidates of the quantumly advantageous functions
a natural candidate for the quantumly advantageous functions is the functions relevant to the hardest
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' proposal of candidates; no proof or experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that proving unconditionally, without a computational hardness assumption, that quantumly advantageous functions exist is a variant of long-standing open problems in complexity theory.
assertions.anchor: New directions of QML, item 3, p.4-5
quotes: a variant of long-standing open problems in the complexity
unconditionally without any computational hardness assumption
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit on its own result in the New directions section (item 3).
assertions.reader_inference: The separation therefore depends on assuming that a suitable function exists; no concrete function is shown to meet the definition.

assertions.value: The authors state that a large dimension of the feature space is not a prerequisite for the advantage of QML in their framework, as opposed to a common unproven folklore.
quotes: a large dimension of the feature space is not even a prerequisite for the advantage of QML in our framework
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion the authors draw from their theorem, in the Discussion.

assertions.value: The authors state that an experimental challenge remains in realizing quantum computation that surpasses the capability of classical computation, and that the paper reports no experimental demonstration.
quotes: an experimental challenge still remains in seeking how to realize quantum computation to surpass the capability of classical computation
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a remaining limit (Discussion).
assertions.reader_inference: The paper contains no experiments or numerical results; every result is a proof.
